cornish-game-hen-roasted-skin-eaten.title: Cornish Game Hen, Roasted, Skin Eaten

content.title: About
content.content: The Cornish game hen is a small domestic bird, typically weighing 400–600 g. When roasted, the skin stays crisp and edible, while the meat remains tender and flavorful. It is often served whole in restaurants and at festive meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cornish game hens were developed in England in the 19th century as ornamental bantam chickens.
They reach only about 30 cm in height, making them quick to cook.
The meat is considered more tender than that of standard chickens because of its high protein and low fat content.
Traditionally they are roasted whole, frequently stuffed with herbs, lemon, and garlic.
In the United States the bird is commonly called “Cornish game hen,” although it is not a game bird.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of roasted cornish hen provides about 24 g of high‑quality protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other poultry, the cornish hen contains relatively little fat, especially when the skin is kept crisp but not over‑fried.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat is a good source of niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Does not cause a rapid spike in blood sugar, making it suitable for those monitoring glycemic response.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird proteins.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: As with any meat, it should be cooked to an internal temperature of 74 °C to prevent salmonella.

items.title: High sodium in marinades
items.content: If the bird is pre‑marinated in salty solutions, sodium intake should be considered.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted cornish hen is served whole, then cut into portions. The skin is edible and adds a pleasant crunch. The meat pairs well with herbs, lemon, garlic, and sauces such as butter‑based gravies or yogurt‑based dressings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh meat should be kept in the refrigerator at +2–4 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen meat can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge before cooking, never at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Masa harina is a pre‑cooked corn flour made from dried corn kernels that have been cooked, dried and ground. It is a staple in Mexican cuisine for making tortillas, tamales, enchiladas and other traditional dishes. The cooked flour has a soft texture and a distinctive corn aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Masa harina is traditionally made from yellow corn, but white and blue varieties also exist.
The process involves cooking the kernels in an alkaline solution (nixtamalization), which enhances flavor and nutritional value.
Mexico is the world’s largest consumer and producer of masa harina.
Masa harina is used beyond Mexican cuisine, appearing in Guatemalan and Peruvian dishes as well.
There is a “cooked” version that has already been thermally treated and is ready to use without additional mixing.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Masa harina provides slowly digestible carbs that deliver steady energy.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with wheat flour, masa harina contains very little fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Corn fiber supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Ideal for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: Sodium content in ready‑made masa
items.content: Prepared masa can be salted; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn products can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume them in moderation.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Cooked masa harina is used to quickly make tortillas, tamales, enchiladas, and as a base for soups or casseroles. Simply hydrate a small amount with water, knead to the desired consistency, and shape the dough.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the masa harina package in a cool, dry place, sealed tightly. After opening, store in the refrigerator and use within 2–3 days.

meat-substitute-cereal-and-vegetable-pro.title: Meat substitute, cereal- and vegetable protein-based, fried

content.title: About
content.content: The meat substitute, cereal- and vegetable protein-based, fried, is a plant‑based protein product made from a blend of cereals (wheat, rice, corn) and vegetable proteins (soy, pea). It is fried to a golden crust, giving a crunchy texture and a flavor reminiscent of traditional meat snacks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product is completely vegan and contains no animal ingredients.
Cereal and legume proteins are combined to provide a complete amino‑acid profile comparable to meat.
Frying is done with minimal oil, preserving crunch while keeping calories lower.
It is often used in vegetarian and vegan versions of dishes, replacing patties, nuggets, and sticks.
Fiber content is higher than most meat analogues, supporting digestion.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Provides 15–20 % protein, helping maintain muscle mass and satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Most fats are polyunsaturated, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids gut function and helps stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Fortified with thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Cholesterol‑free
items.content: Contains no cholesterol, making it safe for people with elevated lipid levels.

items.title: Soy and pea protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy or pea may experience reactions, up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: If wheat is used, the product is not suitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Some versions may contain higher sodium or flavor enhancers, which should be considered in a restricted diet.

items.title: Processed ingredients
items.content: As with many ready‑made foods, it may contain preservatives; choose options without artificial additives when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, vegetarian burgers, soups, or used as a coating for vegetables. For best texture, reheat in the oven or skillet until crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a sealed package. After opening, consume within 2–3 days or keep refrigerated for up to a week. Discard if a rancid odor develops.

content.title: About
content.content: Sushi is a traditional Japanese dish consisting of vinegared rice combined with various fillings such as raw fish, seafood, vegetables, and omelette. It is served as rolls (maki), nigiri (rice topped with a slice of fish), or sashimi (just the fish without rice).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest references to sushi date back to the 8th century in Japan, where it was a method of preserving fish.
There are more than 200 types of sushi, including maki, nigiri, uramaki, and tempura rolls.
Traditional sushi rice is seasoned with rice vinegar, sugar, and salt, giving it a characteristic sweet‑sour flavor.
In Japan sushi is commonly eaten with soy sauce, wasabi, and pickled ginger, which cleanse the palate between bites.
Sushi became popular outside Japan in the 1970s when the first sushi restaurants opened in the United States.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Raw fish used in sushi contains EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A single piece of sushi typically contains 30–50 kcal, making it a convenient snack for weight control.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Fish and seafood provide high‑quality complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna, salmon, and sea bass are rich in vitamin B12, essential for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Rice, vinegar, and seaweed (nori) promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Risk of foodborne infections
items.content: Raw fish can harbor parasites and bacteria; only fish that has been inspected and approved for raw consumption should be used.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and pickled ginger can increase sodium intake, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Seafood allergies
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, shellfish, or crustaceans.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Certain fish such as mackerel and tuna may contain mercury; pregnant women and children should limit their consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sushi is typically picked up with chopsticks or by hand, dipped lightly (1–2 cm) into soy sauce, a small dab of wasabi may be added, and eaten in one bite. Sashimi is served without rice, and rolls are usually cut into 6–8 pieces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared sushi should be kept in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C and consumed within 24 hours. The rice quickly loses its texture and the fish loses freshness. Discard sushi if the fish smells sour or appears discolored.
